clue.text: Excessive travel to the next valley may be considered this

definitions.text: travel to the next valley may be considered this
definitions.meaning: crossing a ridge into the next valley literally takes you up and across the summit

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for going too far is borrowed from soldiers climbing out of trenches; literally it is crossing a hill's summit.

clue.text: Somersaults, top coming off? Oh dear!

indicators.note: the top of a down entry is its first letter, which is removed here

parts.note: loops are aerial somersaults, as by a stunt plane

explanation.surface: A gymnast's somersaults go wrong and the onlooker exclaims in dismay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top coming off' takes the first letter L off LOOPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of dismay at a small mistake or accident.

clue.text: Former lover is coming in absolutely beautiful

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: signals that one word goes inside another

parts.note: quite can mean absolutely, as in 'quite right'
taken as written

explanation.surface: An ex-partner arrives looking utterly gorgeous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former lover' reads as a person in the scene, but it simply supplies the standard two-letter short form for an ex-partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Exquisite describes something of extreme, delicate beauty, a close synonym.

clue.text: Shakespeare's version of Christmas story?

parts.note: a story set at Christmas would be a seasonal tale, and one of Shakespeare's late plays has such a seasonal title

explanation.definitionFit: The play's title names a tale told in the cold season, which a Christmas story would be.

clue.text: Sharing experiences upset me — a course ending in melancholy

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the two letters of 'me' are turned about

parts.note: a path is a course or route

indicators.note: points to the final letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A gloomy student is upset by a course that ends sadly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns ME into EM; then A, PATH and Y, the last letter of melancholy ('ending in').
explanation.definitionFit: Empathy is the ability to share and understand another person's feelings.

clue.text: Unable to row, as loser at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A losing rower out on the water cannot row any more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' rearranges AS LOSER.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat without oars cannot be rowed, so its crew is literally unable to row.

clue.text: Northerner finding local writer interminable?

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: Sir Walter Scott was a novelist of Scotland, local to a Scottish northerner

explanation.surface: A man from the north discovers a regional author who never stops writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Walter Scott was a Scottish novelist; 'interminable' takes the last T off SCOTT.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland is the northern part of Britain, so a Scot is a northerner from a British viewpoint.

clue.text: Youngster told off around start of lesson

indicators.note: means the first piece encloses the second

parts.note: chid is an old past tense of chide, to scold

indicators.note: points to the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A pupil is scolded at the beginning of a class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts L, the 'start of' lesson, inside CHID, an old past tense of chide.
explanation.definitionFit: A child is a young person, so it is a straightforward synonym for youngster.

clue.text: Unknown to jeer after getting access to theatre? Absolutely right

indicators.note: places the following pieces after the one named next

parts.note: a ticket gets you into a theatre
y is an algebraic unknown
to boo is to jeer

explanation.surface: A theatregoer who just got a ticket stays quiet about wanting to heckle.
explanation.walkthrough: Tickety-boo is British slang for fine or in order; 'access to theatre' is a cryptic way of describing what admits you.
explanation.definitionFit: Tickety-boo is informal British slang meaning everything is fine and in order.

clue.text: Wrongly inside, convict's short time there is purposeless

indicators.note: there points back to the jumbled word as the place where the next pieces go
wrongly means in error, so these letters are rearranged
short means cut off, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a convict is a criminal

explanation.surface: A wrongly jailed prisoner serves a short sentence that achieves nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' looks like prison slang for being jailed, matching 'convict', but it is the anagram fodder; 'there' sends the shortened convict and time into the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiscriminate action is random, done without careful choice or aim.

clue.text: Card game unfinished? Show of annoyance

indicators.note: means the last letter is left off

parts.note: piquet is a two-player card game

explanation.surface: A player storms off in a huff before a card game is over.
explanation.walkthrough: Piquet is an old two-player card game; 'unfinished' drops its final T.
explanation.definitionFit: Pique is resentment from wounded pride, often shown as a fit of irritation.

clue.text: No one held to account after soldier's behaving irrationally

indicators.note: puts the following pieces behind the soldier

parts.note: a para is a paratrooper
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A soldier is acting strangely because nobody has been called to account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held to' simply joins the pieces; 'soldier' in crosswords is often a paratrooper or a GI.
explanation.definitionFit: A paranoiac is gripped by irrational suspicion, so the word describes someone behaving irrationally.

clue.text: Central supplier of pork and game?

definitions.meaning: an animal that gives pork, standing in the centre
a children's game where one player in the middle tries to intercept a ball thrown between two others

explanation.definitionFit: The playground game is named after the player stuck in the middle, and pigs supply pork.

clue.text: A couple of lines used in summing up

definitions.text: A couple of lines used in summing up

parts.words: A couple of lines used in summing up
parts.note: reads like a short concluding remark, but means two parallel strokes written in an arithmetic sum

explanation.definitionFit: The mathematical symbol is two short parallel lines, written in a sum before the total.

clue.text: Question that is posed by odd bits of telly, offering little controversy

parts.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, that is

indicators.note: means the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A question raised by fragments of a TV programme causes little stir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd bits of' telly gives T, L and Y, its first, third and fifth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something quietly means without fuss or noise, so attracting little dispute.

clue.text: Thus financial centre will welcome in energy corporation

parts.note: so means thus

indicators.note: signals that the first piece takes the second inside it

parts.note: the City is London's financial district
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: The financial district is set to welcome an energy company.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district; 'will welcome in' puts E inside CITY.
explanation.definitionFit: A society can be an incorporated body or association, so a corporation in that sense.

clue.text: Material appearing mysterious, so I create anew

indicators.note: making something anew means rearranging these letters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An artist says that unclear material inspires fresh work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anew' rearranges SO I CREATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoterica are obscure items understood only by a few, so mysterious material.

clue.text: Claimed article was wrong about verse

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
erred means was wrong

explanation.surface: Someone insisted a magazine piece got its poetry wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts ERRED around V, after A.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to state firmly, so averred means asserted or claimed.

clue.text: Mammals or marsupials initially used in gamble

indicators.note: signals that the next pieces are set inside the gamble

parts.note: to dice is to gamble
taken as written

indicators.note: means the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Zoologists bet on which mammals or marsupials will turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gamble' looks like a noun but is the verb to dice; marsupials only supplies its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Dormice are small rodents, which are mammals.

clue.text: Who gets any benefit from studying Latin?

definitions.text: Who gets any benefit from studying Latin?

parts.words: Who gets any benefit from studying Latin?
parts.note: reads as doubting the use of classics lessons, but is a Latin question about who stands to profit

explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase asks who benefits, used when looking for a motive.

clue.text: Sheep found in central procession

indicators.note: signals that one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: core means central, as in core values
a teg is a sheep in its second year

explanation.surface: A sheep wanders into the middle of a parade.
explanation.walkthrough: A teg is a dialect word for a sheep in its second year, worth knowing for crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A cortege is a solemn procession, especially at a funeral.

clue.text: Inclined to forget instruction to get in bread?

parts.note: scatter is an order to jumble; jumbling the letters of brained gives in bread

explanation.surface: An absent-minded baker needs an instruction to put the bread in.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an instruction: scatter the letters of BRAINED and you get IN BREAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A scatterbrained person is disorganised and forgetful.

clue.text: Brightest star in the final phase

indicators.note: signals the letters run inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: The brightest star shines in the last stage of a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the letters inside 'final phase'.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronomers label the brightest star of a constellation with the first Greek letter.

clue.text: Unknown child turning up with lots of questions

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up reads a word from bottom to top

parts.note: a son is a child
y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A strange child appears and keeps asking questions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' applies to the child alone; the unknown stays at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone nosy is inquisitive, always asking questions about others.

clue.text: I have to follow one dreadful slump, responding promptly

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: dreadful means awful, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: Someone adds that they have lived through one terrible downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to follow' places the contraction after the rest; 'one dreadful slump' reads like an economic report.
explanation.definitionFit: Impulsive behaviour is acting on sudden urges, reacting at once without reflection.

clue.text: Am I ready for a friend?

parts.note: taken as written
go can mean ready, as in all systems go

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they are prepared to be a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: GO for ready comes from launch talk, where 'all systems go' means ready.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend, also used informally in English.

clue.text: Well-trimmed farm animals

explanation.definitionFit: Neat means tidy; as an old noun it means cattle, as in neatherd and neat's-foot oil.

clue.text: Immoral behaviour, say, in valley's risqu

indicators.note: signals the example goes inside the valley

parts.note: a dene is a small wooded valley
e.g. means for example, which say can mean
risqué means racy

explanation.surface: Bawdy conduct is found in a risqué valley.
explanation.walkthrough: The last word is risqué, its accent lost in the text; DENE is a northern English word for a valley.
explanation.definitionFit: Degeneracy is moral decline, so it describes debased, immoral conduct.
